::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Confirm your installation works; read a real Movebank file; find out
what is actually in it; compute a fix rate and a fix success rate; plot a
trajectory using nothing but base R.

**Time:** ~50 minutes. **Packages:** none — base R only, on purpose.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
Work inside the course RStudio project (`animtrack-2627.Rproj`). Then the path
`data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz` resolves without you editing anything.
:::

## Task 0 — Does your installation work?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sessionInfo()

need <- c("sf", "terra", "move2", "amt", "adehabitatHR", "ctmm",
          "moveHMM", "survival", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "mapview")
for (p in need) {
  ok <- requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("%-14s %s\n", p, if (ok) as.character(packageVersion(p)) else "** MISSING **"))
}
```
:::


If anything says `MISSING`, go back to the [setup page](../../setup.qmd) now —
you will need all of these by Class 3.

## Task 1 — Read the data

R reads gzipped CSV directly. No need to decompress anything.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dim(buffalo)
#> [1] 28410    18
names(buffalo)
#>  [1] "event.id"                        "visible"                        
#>  [3] "timestamp"                       "location.long"                  
#>  [5] "location.lat"                    "behavioural.classification"     
#>  [7] "comments"                        "manually.marked.outlier"        
#>  [9] "sensor.type"                     "individual.taxon.canonical.name"
#> [11] "tag.local.identifier"            "individual.local.identifier"    
#> [13] "study.name"                      "utm.easting"                    
#> [15] "utm.northing"                    "utm.zone"                       
#> [17] "study.timezone"                  "study.local.timestamp"
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why did the column names change?

Movebank uses hyphens: `location-long`. R identifiers cannot contain hyphens,
so `read.csv()` converts them to dots by default: `location.long`. You can
keep the originals with `check.names = FALSE`, but then you need backticks
everywhere — not worth it.
:::

### Your turn

**1a.** How many rows? How many columns?
**1b.** How many individual animals, and what are they called?
**1c.** What species, and what sensor type?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(buffalo)
#> [1] 28410
ncol(buffalo)
#> [1] 18

unique(buffalo$individual.local.identifier)
#> [1] "Queen"  "Gabs"   "Cilla"  "Mvubu"  "Toni"   "Pepper"
length(unique(buffalo$individual.local.identifier))
#> [1] 6

unique(buffalo$individual.taxon.canonical.name)
#> [1] "Syncerus caffer"
unique(buffalo$sensor.type)
#> [1] "gps"
```
:::


Six buffalo, GPS-collared. Note that `table()` is more informative than
`unique()` when you also want the number of fixes per animal:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
table(buffalo$individual.local.identifier)
#> 
#>  Cilla   Gabs  Mvubu Pepper  Queen   Toni 
#>   3556   4831   3491   5163   4997   6372
```
:::


Already a lesson: the animals are **not** equally sampled. Any summary that
pools them without accounting for that is dominated by whichever individual
contributed most fixes.
:::

## Task 2 — Timestamps are not text

This is the single most important line of code in the whole course.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
buffalo$t <- as.POSIXct(buffalo$timestamp, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")

class(buffalo$t)
#> [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt"
range(buffalo$t)
#> [1] "2005-02-17 05:05:00 UTC" "2006-12-31 14:34:00 UTC"
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## Always set `tz`

If you omit `tz`, R silently uses **your computer's** time zone. Your analysis
then gives different answers on a laptop in Rome and a server in California.
Movebank timestamps are UTC. Say so.
:::

### Your turn

**2a.** Over how many days does the study run?
**2b.** In which months are there most fixes?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
difftime(max(buffalo$t), min(buffalo$t), units = "days")
#> Time difference of 682.3951 days

table(format(buffalo$t, "%Y-%m"))
#> 
#> 2005-02 2005-03 2005-04 2005-05 2005-06 2005-07 2005-08 2005-09 2005-10 2005-11 
#>     289     752    1290     887     889    1190    3220    4186    4192    3704 
#> 2005-12 2006-01 2006-02 2006-03 2006-04 2006-05 2006-06 2006-07 2006-08 2006-09 
#>    2574    1425     841     737     626     582     235     197     147     138 
#> 2006-10 2006-11 2006-12 
#>     108     140      61
```
:::


The monthly counts are very uneven — collars were deployed and failed at
different times. This matters: a "seasonal" pattern can easily be a deployment
pattern in disguise.
:::

## Task 3 — Subset one animal and sort it

Almost every movement calculation assumes the rows are **one individual, in
time order**. Never assume a file arrives sorted.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
queen <- buffalo[buffalo$individual.local.identifier == "Queen", ]
queen <- queen[order(queen$t), ]

nrow(queen)
#> [1] 4997
head(queen[, c("t", "location.long", "location.lat")])
#>                     t location.long location.lat
#> 1 2005-02-17 05:05:00      31.76642    -24.53730
#> 2 2005-02-17 05:05:00      31.76642    -24.53730
#> 3 2005-02-17 06:08:00      31.76442    -24.53931
#> 4 2005-02-17 06:08:00      31.76442    -24.53931
#> 5 2005-02-17 07:05:00      31.76114    -24.54799
#> 6 2005-02-17 08:05:00      31.76080    -24.54703
```
:::


### Your turn

**3a.** Were the rows already in time order?
**3b.** Are there repeated timestamps?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Was the original order already sorted in time?
queen_raw <- buffalo[buffalo$individual.local.identifier == "Queen", ]
is.unsorted(queen_raw$t)
#> [1] FALSE

# Repeated timestamps?
sum(duplicated(queen$t))
#> [1] 452
```
:::


There are duplicated timestamps — the collar transmitted the same fix more
than once. Across the whole file:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(duplicated(buffalo[, c("individual.local.identifier", "timestamp")]))
#> [1] 3747
```
:::


Roughly 13% of the file. We will remove these properly in Class 3; today just
register that **real data arrive dirty**, and that you only find out by
looking.
:::

## Task 4 — Fix interval and fix success

The collar was *programmed* to attempt a fix on a schedule. What did it
actually deliver?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Drop duplicated timestamps first, or every duplicate creates a zero-length interval
queen_u <- queen[!duplicated(queen$t), ]

dt <- as.numeric(diff(queen_u$t), units = "hours")

summary(dt)
#>      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
#> 3.333e-02 1.000e+00 1.000e+00 2.445e+00 1.000e+00 2.523e+03
```
:::


### Your turn

**4a.** What is the *modal* (most common) interval? That is the programmed fix rate.
**4b.** What fraction of intervals are exactly that? This is your fix success rate.
**4c.** What is the longest gap, and what might explain it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Round to the nearest 0.1 h so near-identical intervals group together
tab <- sort(table(round(dt, 1)), decreasing = TRUE)
head(tab, 5)
#> 
#>    1  0.9    0    2  0.1 
#> 4203  120   55   42   35

modal_dt <- as.numeric(names(tab)[1])
modal_dt
#> [1] 1

# Proportion of intervals at the programmed rate
mean(abs(dt - modal_dt) < 0.1)
#> [1] 0.9515845

# The worst gap, in days
max(dt) / 24
#> [1] 105.1167
```
:::


The modal interval is the programmed schedule. Everything longer is a
**missed fix** — the collar tried and failed, or was off.

Long gaps have mundane explanations that matter enormously: battery
saving schedules, the animal under dense canopy or in a gorge, the collar
temporarily upside-down, or the animal dead and the collar lying face-down.

A cleaner way to count missed fixes — how many scheduled attempts fit in
each observed gap:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
missed <- round(dt / modal_dt) - 1
sum(missed)
#> [1] 6563
sum(missed) / (nrow(queen_u) + sum(missed))   # overall failure rate
#> [1] 0.5908354
```
:::

:::

## Task 5 — Your first trajectory plot

No spatial packages. Just points and lines.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(queen_u$location.long, queen_u$location.lat,
     type = "l", col = "grey60",
     xlab = "Longitude (°)", ylab = "Latitude (°)",
     main = "Buffalo 'Queen', Kruger NP",
     asp = 1)
points(queen_u$location.long, queen_u$location.lat,
       pch = 16, cex = 0.3, col = "#1f6f78")
points(queen_u$location.long[1], queen_u$location.lat[1],
       pch = 17, cex = 1.6, col = "forestgreen")     # start
points(tail(queen_u$location.long, 1), tail(queen_u$location.lat, 1),
       pch = 15, cex = 1.6, col = "firebrick")       # end
legend("topright", c("start", "end"), pch = c(17, 15),
       col = c("forestgreen", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## This plot is wrong, and knowing why is the point

`asp = 1` forces one degree of longitude to occupy the same screen distance as
one degree of latitude. On the ground at 24°S, one degree of latitude is about
111 km, but one degree of longitude is only about
101 km — the map is stretched
east–west by roughly a factor of 1.1.

At 24° the distortion is modest. Try the same plot for the vulture, which
ranges from 7°N to 54°N, and it becomes severe.

Distances computed from raw degrees are meaningless. Fixing this — properly,
with coordinate reference systems — is [Class 2](../class-02/slides.qmd).
:::

### Your turn

**5a.** Plot all six buffalo on one figure, one colour each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
b <- buffalo[!duplicated(buffalo[, c("individual.local.identifier", "timestamp")]), ]
ids <- unique(b$individual.local.identifier)
cols <- hcl.colors(length(ids), "Dark 3")

plot(b$location.long, b$location.lat, type = "n", asp = 1,
     xlab = "Longitude (°)", ylab = "Latitude (°)",
     main = "Six buffalo, Kruger National Park")

for (i in seq_along(ids)) {
  d <- b[b$individual.local.identifier == ids[i], ]
  d <- d[order(d$t), ]
  lines(d$location.long, d$location.lat, col = cols[i], lwd = 1)
}
legend("topleft", legend = ids, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=720}
:::
:::


The individuals overlap heavily but are not identical — the raw material of
every question in this course. Do they use the same areas at the same *times*?
Do they avoid each other? Do they respond to the same rivers?
:::

## Task 6 — A different animal, a different problem


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
vulture <- read.csv("data/vulture_leo.csv.gz", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
vulture$t <- as.POSIXct(vulture$timestamp, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")
vulture <- vulture[order(vulture$t), ]

plot(vulture$location.long, vulture$location.lat, type = "l",
     col = "grey50", asp = 1,
     xlab = "Longitude (°)", ylab = "Latitude (°)",
     main = "Turkey vulture 'Leo', 2007-2013")
points(vulture$location.long, vulture$location.lat,
       pch = 16, cex = 0.15, col = "#c1440e")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


### Your turn

**6a.** Why would a single home-range estimate for this animal be meaningless?
**6b.** Plot latitude against time. What do you see?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(vulture$t, vulture$location.lat, type = "l",
     col = "#c1440e", xlab = "", ylab = "Latitude (°)",
     main = "Latitude over time — six annual migrations")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::
:::


A clean sawtooth. Leo is not doing one thing: he alternates between two
residency phases (Canada, South America) and two directed migrations, and
repeats that six times.

A home range computed over the whole track would describe an "area of use"
spanning two continents — an area the animal essentially never occupies. It
would be arithmetically correct and biologically meaningless.

This is exactly the motivation for [Class 6](../class-06/slides.qmd):
**segment first, then analyse**. Note also that latitude-over-time is a
remarkably effective diagnostic plot — always look at your coordinates against
time before you model anything.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
You compute `diff(t)` on a data frame you forgot to sort by time. What do you
get?

- [ ] An error
- [x] A mixture of positive and negative intervals, and nonsense summaries
- [ ] Correct intervals — `diff()` sorts internally
- [ ] All zeros

::: {.quiz-feedback}
`diff()` does exactly what you asked: it subtracts each element from the next,
in the order given. Out of order, you get negative time differences, and any
speed you compute from them is garbage — often silently, because `summary()`
still returns numbers.

**Always `order(t)` within individual before any step calculation.** This is
the most common error in beginner movement code.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
A collar programmed for hourly fixes returns 14,000 fixes over exactly two
years. Roughly what was the fix success rate?

- [ ] ~100%
- [x] ~80%
- [ ] ~50%
- [ ] Impossible to say without the DOP values

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Two years of hourly attempts is 2 × 365 × 24 ≈ 17,520. So 14,000 / 17,520 ≈
**80%**, which is a fairly typical figure for a GPS collar on a large mammal
in mixed habitat.

The 20% that failed is not noise: if failures concentrate in closed habitat,
your data under-represent exactly the places the animal may prefer.
:::
:::

## Before Class 2

- Make sure `library(sf)` and `library(terra)` both load without errors.
- Look at the [Datasets page](../../data.qmd) so the three files are familiar.
- Optional but useful: skim
  [Geocomputation with R, chapter 2](https://r.geocompx.org/spatial-class).
